ferrari.name: Ferrari
ferrari.notes: The only constructor to have contested every season since 1950. Fifteen drivers' titles and sixteen constructors' titles, the last in 2008. Won its first championship Grand Prix at Silverstone in 1951 with Gonzalez.

mercedes.name: Mercedes
mercedes.notes: Two spells: a works team in 1954-55 that won two titles with Fangio and withdrew after Le Mans, and the modern operation that took over Brawn GP in 2010 and won eight consecutive constructors' championships from 2014. Registered first entry 1954; the current entity traces its entry chain through BAR and Honda.

mclaren.name: McLaren
mclaren.notes: Founded by Bruce McLaren in 1963, first entry 1966. Second only to Ferrari in wins and titles. The MP4/4 of 1988 won 15 of 16 races. Returned to the top in 2024-25 after a 26-year constructors' drought.

red-bull.name: Red Bull Racing
red-bull.notes: Bought the Jaguar entry for a nominal sum in late 2004. Six constructors' titles and eight drivers' titles in twenty seasons. Its 2023 season — 21 wins from 22 — is the most dominant in the sport's history.

williams.name: Williams
williams.notes: Frank Williams's second and lasting venture. Nine constructors' titles, all between 1980 and 1997. Sold to Dorilton Capital in 2020, ending family control.

alpine.name: Alpine
alpine.notes: The Renault works entry rebadged for 2021. One win, at the 2021 Hungarian GP with Ocon. The Enstone factory it occupies has won two constructors' titles under earlier names.

aston-martin.name: Aston Martin
aston-martin.full_name: Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team
aston-martin.notes: Two spells. Aston Martin entered the front-engined DBR4 and DBR5 in 1959-60, by which time the rear-engined Coopers had made them obsolete; the marque scored no points. The current entity is unrelated, dating from Lawrence Stroll's 2021 rebrand of Racing Point. Adrian Newey joined as team principal for 2026.

2022.entrant_name: Aston Martin Aramco Cognizant F1 Team

2023.entrant_name: Aston Martin Aramco Cognizant F1 Team

2026.entrant_name: Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team

haas.name: Haas F1 Team
haas.notes: The first American constructor since 1986, and the first to run a customer-parts model built around Ferrari supply and Dallara manufacture.

racing-bulls.name: Racing Bulls
racing-bulls.full_name: Visa Cash App Racing Bulls Formula One Team
racing-bulls.notes: The Faenza entry, continuously in the championship since Minardi's 1985 debut. Two wins, both giant-killings: Vettel at Monza in 2008 and Gasly at Monza in 2020. The Faenza team's two wins are credited to the constructor names it raced under at the time, Toro Rosso (2008) and AlphaTauri (2020).

2024.entrant_name: Visa Cash App RB F1 Team

2025.entrant_name: Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 Team

2026.entrant_name: Visa Cash App Racing Bulls Formula One Team

audi.name: Audi
audi.notes: The Hinwil operation founded by Peter Sauber, taken over completely by Audi for the 2026 regulations. Audi builds its own power unit at Neuburg an der Donau — the first new works manufacturer entry since Honda's return.

cadillac.name: Cadillac
cadillac.notes: The eleventh team, admitted for 2026 after a protracted approval process originally begun as the Andretti-Cadillac bid. Runs Ferrari power units pending its own General Motors unit.

lotus.name: Team Lotus
lotus.notes: Colin Chapman's constructor: the monocoque chassis (Lotus 25), full ground effect (Lotus 78/79), active suspension and the first major commercial sponsorship deal. Collapsed in 1994 after Chapman's death in 1982.

brabham.name: Brabham
brabham.notes: Founded by Jack Brabham and Ron Tauranac. Later run by Bernie Ecclestone, whose ownership was the platform for his takeover of the sport's commercial rights. The BT46B 'fan car' won its only race and was withdrawn.

tyrrell.name: Tyrrell
tyrrell.notes: Ken Tyrrell's team, which built the six-wheeled P34. Sold to British American Tobacco in 1997 and became BAR.

1977.entrant_name: First National City Elf Team Tyrrell

1978.entrant_name: First National City Elf Team Tyrrell

cooper.name: Cooper
cooper.notes: Put the engine behind the driver and made the front-engined Grand Prix car obsolete within three seasons.

brm.name: BRM
brm.notes: A national-effort project that took eleven years to win a championship. Built the extraordinary H16 engine.

matra.name: Matra
matra.notes: An aerospace company that won the title at its third attempt, run in 1969 by Ken Tyrrell with Ford power. Its first championship entries were the Formula Two cars admitted to the 1966 German Grand Prix.

vanwall.name: Vanwall
vanwall.notes: Tony Vandervell's team won the first Constructors' Championship in 1958 and withdrew almost immediately after Stuart Lewis-Evans's death.

benetton.name: Benetton
benetton.notes: Bought Toleman in 1985. Michael Schumacher's first two titles came here; the team's 1994 season was dogged by technical-compliance disputes.

renault.name: Renault
renault.notes: Introduced the turbocharged engine to F1 in 1977 and won two doubles with Alonso in 2005-06 after buying Benetton. Withdrew as a works entrant at the end of 2020, rebranding as Alpine.

brawn.name: Brawn GP
brawn.notes: Ross Brawn's management buyout of Honda's abandoned team for a nominal sum. Won both championships in its only season and was sold to Mercedes.

alfa-romeo.name: Alfa Romeo
alfa-romeo.notes: Dominated 1950-51 with the pre-war 158/159 'Alfetta' and won the first two drivers' titles, then withdrew. Returned as a constructor 1979-85 and later as a naming-rights partner to Sauber, 2019-2023.

maserati.name: Maserati
maserati.notes: The 250F is among the most admired Grand Prix cars ever built; Fangio took the 1957 title in one.

ligier.name: Ligier
ligier.notes: Guy Ligier's team; sold to Alain Prost in 1997.

jordan.name: Jordan
jordan.notes: Eddie Jordan's team gave Michael Schumacher his F1 debut at Spa in 1991 and finished third in the 1999 championship.

march.name: March
march.notes: A customer-car manufacturer that also ran a works entry; Peterson and Lauda both started here.

1975.entrant_name: First National City Bank Team Penske

wolf.name: Walter Wolf Racing
wolf.notes: Won on its championship debut in Argentina 1977 with Scheckter — a feat matched only by Brawn GP.

hesketh.name: Hesketh
hesketh.notes: Lord Hesketh's unsponsored team won the 1975 Dutch GP with James Hunt.

shadow.name: Shadow
shadow.notes: Won the 1977 Austrian GP with Alan Jones. A staff walkout founded Arrows.

penske.name: Penske
penske.notes: Won the 1976 Austrian GP with John Watson, then left for American racing. The PC4 raced on into 1977 in other hands - ATS Racing and Interscope - which is why the constructor's last entry is a year after the team's.

1975.entrant_name: First National City Bank Team Penske

1976.entrant_name: First National City Bank Team Penske

stewart-gp.name: Stewart Grand Prix
stewart-gp.notes: Jackie and Paul Stewart's Ford-backed team won at the Nurburgring in 1999 and was sold to Ford to become Jaguar.

jaguar.name: Jaguar Racing
jaguar.notes: Ford's rebadging of Stewart. Never won a race; sold to Red Bull for a nominal sum in 2004.

honda-works.name: Honda
honda-works.notes: Two spells as a constructor: 1964-68, winning in Mexico 1965 and Monza 1967, and 2006-08 after buying BAR. Withdrew in the 2008 financial crisis, whereupon the team became Brawn GP.

2006.entrant_name: Lucky Strike Honda Racing F1 Team

bar.name: British American Racing
bar.notes: Built from the Tyrrell entry with British American Tobacco money. Second in the 2004 constructors' championship.

toro-rosso.name: Scuderia Toro Rosso
toro-rosso.notes: Red Bull's junior team; Vettel's Monza 2008 win remains the last for a team using a customer chassis philosophy of that kind.

alphatauri.name: Scuderia AlphaTauri
alphatauri.notes: The Faenza team rebranded to promote Red Bull's fashion label. Gasly won at Monza in 2020.

force-india.name: Force India
force-india.notes: Vijay Mallya's team took pole and a podium at Spa in 2009 and finished fourth in 2016 and 2017 before going into administration.

2016.entrant_name: Sahara Force India Formula One Team

2018.entrant_name: Racing Point Force India F1 Team

racing-point.name: Racing Point
racing-point.notes: Won the 2020 Sakhir GP with Perez. Penalised that year for copying Mercedes brake ducts — the 'pink Mercedes' affair.

sauber.name: Sauber
sauber.notes: Peter Sauber's independent team. Its single win came as BMW Sauber with Kubica in Canada 2008. Ran as Alfa Romeo 2019-23 and Kick Sauber 2024-25 before becoming Audi. Its single victory is credited to BMW Sauber, the constructor name in use in 2008.

bmw-sauber.name: BMW Sauber
bmw-sauber.notes: BMW's works entry, second in the 2007 constructors' championship. Withdrew after 2009.

lotus-f1.name: Lotus F1 Team
lotus-f1.notes: The Enstone team under Genii Capital ownership, using the Lotus name by licence. Raikkonen won in Abu Dhabi 2012 and Australia 2013.

toyota.name: Toyota
toyota.notes: The largest budget in the sport for much of its run and no wins from 139 starts. Withdrew after 2009.

minardi.name: Minardi
minardi.notes: The Faenza team's original identity; a proving ground for Alonso, Trulli, Fisichella and Webber. Sold to Red Bull in 2005.

arrows.name: Arrows
arrows.notes: 382 starts without a win — the most of any constructor. Came closest with Damon Hill at the Hungaroring in 1997.

prost-gp.name: Prost Grand Prix
prost-gp.notes: Alain Prost's purchase of Ligier; collapsed in bankruptcy in 2002.

super-aguri.name: Super Aguri
super-aguri.notes: Aguri Suzuki's Honda-backed team; scored a point at Montreal in 2007 and folded mid-2008.

hrt.name: HRT
hrt.notes: One of the three 2010 entrants admitted on the promise of a budget cap that never arrived. Never scored a point.

virgin.name: Virgin Racing / Marussia / Manor
virgin.notes: Ran as Virgin, Marussia and Manor. Jules Bianchi's ninth place at Monaco in 2014 was its only points finish; he was fatally injured at Suzuka that year.

caterham.name: Caterham / Team Lotus (2010-14)
caterham.notes: Entered as Lotus Racing, raced as Team Lotus in 2011 amid a naming dispute with the Enstone team, then as Caterham. Never scored.

toleman.name: Toleman
toleman.notes: Ayrton Senna's first team; his second place in the Monaco rain of 1984 announced him. Sold to Benetton.

1971.entrant_name: Auto Motor und Sport Team Surtees

eagle.name: Eagle
eagle.notes: Dan Gurney won the 1967 Belgian GP in a car of his own construction — one of three men to do so, with Jack Brabham and Bruce McLaren.

porsche.name: Porsche
porsche.notes: Won the 1962 French GP with Dan Gurney. Returned as an engine supplier badged TAG in the 1980s.

lancia.name: Lancia
lancia.notes: The D50 was handed to Ferrari after Ascari's death and won the 1956 title in Fangio's hands as the Lancia-Ferrari.

rob-walker.name: Rob Walker Racing
rob-walker.notes: The most successful private entrant in history: Moss's 1958 Argentine GP win was the first for a mid-engined car and the first for a privateer. Its Grand Prix victories are credited to the Cooper and Lotus chassis it entered, so it holds no constructor win total of its own.

lago.name: Talbot-Lago
lago.notes: Ran the pre-war T26C through the early 1950s. Its naturally aspirated 4.5-litre engine was slower than the supercharged Alfas but drank far less, so a Talbot could sometimes run a race non-stop while the front-runners refuelled twice. Rosier won Spa in 1950 that way.

gordini.name: Gordini
gordini.notes: Amedee Gordini's small team, chronically underfunded and known as 'le sorcier' for extracting results from very little money.

connaught.name: Connaught
connaught.notes: British constructor whose Type B gave Britain one of its first significant Grand Prix results at Syracuse in 1955.

lola.name: Lola
lola.notes: Eric Broadley's constructor, better known for sports and Indycars. Its 1962 Formula One car was run by the Bowmaker team for John Surtees, and the Lola name reappeared as a chassis supplier for decades afterwards.

fittipaldi.name: Fittipaldi
fittipaldi.notes: Emerson Fittipaldi left McLaren as a double champion to drive for his brother Wilson's team. It never won a race and the decision is usually read as the one that ended his career at the front.

larrousse.name: Larrousse
larrousse.notes: Gerard Larrousse's team, which took a surprise podium at Suzuka in 1990 with Aguri Suzuki - the first by a Japanese driver.

leyton.name: Leyton House
leyton.notes: The renamed March team, running Adrian Newey's designs. Ivan Capelli led the 1990 French Grand Prix until nine laps from the end.

onyx.name: Onyx
onyx.notes: Lasted a season and a half and took one podium, Johansson's third at Estoril in 1989.

dallara.name: Dallara
dallara.notes: Better known now as a supplier of chassis to other series; ran its own Formula One entry through Scuderia Italia, taking two podiums.

footwork.name: Footwork
footwork.notes: Arrows under its Japanese owner's name from 1991 to 1996. Held here as a separate register entry because that is how the results were published; it is the same operation as Arrows.

design.designers: Gordon Murray
design.power_note: 520 bhp at 12,000 rpm
design.suspension: Pullrod double wishbones front and rear
design.concept: If a flat-12 is too wide for ground-effect tunnels, make the downforce a different way: extract the air from under the car with a fan
design.innovations: Surface heat exchangers in place of radiators on the original BT46 (which did not work); on the BT46B, an engine-driven fan drawing air from a skirted underbody
design.story: The fan was declared to be for cooling, which was true for about 30 per cent of what it did. Lauda won the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix by half a minute and the car was never raced again: Ecclestone owned Brabham and was building his position in FOCA, and the other team principals made withdrawing it the price. It remains the only car to win every Grand Prix it entered.
design.outcome: The BT46B won the one race it started. The conventional BT46 won at Monza the same year.

design.designers: Colin Chapman (chassis), Frank Costin (aerodynamics), Leo Kuzmicki (engine)
design.power_note: About 290 bhp at 7,500 rpm on methanol; 255-262 bhp under the 1958 pump-fuel rules
design.suspension: Front: torsion bars. Rear: de Dion axle
design.concept: A motorcycle engine multiplied by four in an aircraft-aerodynamicist's body on a Chapman chassis
design.innovations: Bosch fuel injection; Costin's streamlined body, which made it the fastest car in a straight line; four cylinders derived from Norton motorcycle practice
design.story: Tony Vandervell built Vanwall to beat 'those bloody red cars', and did. The 1957 British Grand Prix, shared by Moss and Brooks, was the first World Championship win for a British car. In 1958 Vanwall took the first Constructors' Championship ever awarded - and then Vandervell's health failed and the team effectively stopped, so the first constructors' champion never defended the title.
design.outcome: The first Constructors' Championship, 1958. Six wins that season, three each to Moss and Brooks - and no drivers' title, which went to Hawthorn's Ferrari on consistency.

design.designers: Bob Bell, Pat Symonds, James Allison, Tim Densham, Dino Toso
design.suspension: Pushrod-activated torsion bars front and rear, plus a tuned mass damper in the nose from late 2005
design.concept: A well-balanced car on Michelins, plus a weight on a spring in the nose to stop the front tyres skipping over bumps
design.innovations: The tuned mass damper: a sprung mass in the nose oscillating out of phase with the front suspension, keeping the tyres in contact with the road
design.story: The mass damper was worth about three tenths of a second and was completely legal until the FIA decided in 2006 that a mass that is not rigidly attached counts as a movable aerodynamic device. Renault won the 2005 titles and broke a run of five consecutive Ferrari championships doing it.
design.outcome: 19 races, 8 wins, 7 poles. Alonso's first title, at 24 the youngest champion to that point, and Renault's first constructors' championship.

mclaren-mp4-1.name: MP4/1
mclaren-mp4-1.designers: John Barnard ; Alan Jenkins ; John Baldwin ; Mike Lock ; Collin Smith ; Steve Nichols
mclaren-mp4-1.engine_name: 1981-1983: mid-engine, longitudinally mounted, Ford-Cosworth DFV, 2993 cc, NA, 90° V8; 1983: mid-engine, longitudinally mounted, TAG-Porsche TTE PO1, 1499 cc, turbo, 90° V6
mclaren-mp4-1.power_note: 510 hp @ 11,000 rpm (Cosworth DFY V8), 700 hp @ 11,500 rpm (TAG-Porsche V6 turbo)

design.designers: John Barnard, Alan Jenkins, Steve Nichols
design.power_note: 510 bhp at 11,000 rpm; a TAG-Porsche turbo V6 of about 700 bhp was fitted late in 1983
design.concept: Aluminium is not stiff enough to carry ground-effect loads; build the tub out of carbon fibre instead
design.innovations: The first carbon-fibre composite monocoque to race in Formula One
design.story: Barnard got the idea from Rolls-Royce engineers using carbon fibre in turbofan blades, and had the tub built by Hercules Aerospace in Utah because nobody in motor racing could make one. The paddock thought it would shatter. Then John Watson crashed heavily at Monza in 1981, the car broke apart around a tub that stayed intact, and he walked away. Every car on the grid was carbon-fibre within a few years, and it is the single largest reason drivers stopped dying.
design.outcome: 43 races, 6 wins. No championships - its importance is structural, not competitive.

design.designers: Colin Chapman, Maurice Philippe
design.power_note: 420-440 bhp at 9,000-10,000 rpm through its life
design.suspension: Front: double wishbone with inboard spring/damper. Rear: top link, lower wishbone and radius rods
design.concept: Bolt the engine straight to the back of the tub and let it be the back of the car
design.innovations: The engine as a fully stressed structural member, carrying the rear suspension; and, from 1968, aerofoil wings mounted on struts to the uprights
design.story: Ford paid Cosworth £100,000 to build the DFV and gave Lotus a year of exclusivity. Clark won first time out at Zandvoort. When the exclusivity lapsed the DFV was sold to anyone who asked, and it went on to win 155 Grands Prix - the reason a small British team with no engine of its own could beat Ferrari for the next fifteen years. The 49 also carried the first wings, which appeared at Monaco in 1968 and were mounted so high and so flimsily that two of them collapsed at Montjuic in 1969.
design.outcome: 12 wins, 19 poles. Hill's 1968 title and Rindt's posthumous 1970 title.

design.designers: Gioacchino Colombo
design.power_note: Over 300 bhp as the 158 in 1950; about 420 bhp at 9,600 rpm as the 159 in 1951
design.suspension: Front: trailing arm, transverse leaf springs. Rear: swing axle with transverse leaf spring, replaced by a de Dion axle on the 159
design.concept: A pre-war voiturette design, hidden through the war and brought back to win the first two World Championships
design.innovations: Nothing new: the point of the 158 is that a 1938 design was still the best car in the world in 1951
design.story: Alfa entered 1950 with a car designed twelve years earlier and won every race it started. By 1951 it was drinking fuel at about 1.5 miles per gallon and needed two stops where the Ferrari 375 needed one; Fangio won the title anyway, at Barcelona, when Ferrari picked the wrong tyre size. Alfa then withdrew from Grand Prix racing entirely rather than build a successor, which is why 1952 and 1953 were run to Formula Two rules.
design.outcome: Every race entered in 1950; 4 of 7 in 1951. Drivers' titles for Farina and Fangio.

design.designers: Mauro Forghieri
design.chassis_type: steel tube frame with aluminium shear panels
design.suspension: Front and rear double wishbone, front inboard spring/damper
design.concept: Turn the gearbox sideways and put it ahead of the rear axle line: the mass moves forward and the car turns better
design.innovations: The transverse gearbox - the T in the name is trasversale - which concentrated mass within the wheelbase
design.story: The 312T line ran for six seasons and five designations and is the most successful thing Ferrari built before the Schumacher era. The 312T2 is the car Lauda crashed at the Nürburgring in 1976 and the car he was back in six weeks later. By the 312T5 in 1980 the flat-12 was too wide for ground effect and the car was hopeless - Ferrari finished tenth in the championship, and went turbo.
design.outcome: 89 races, 27 wins, 19 poles. Drivers' titles for Lauda (1975, 1977) and Scheckter (1979); constructors' in 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1979.

design.power_note: 750 bhp at 18,000 rpm, the regulation rev limit
design.chassis_type: carbon-fibre and honeycomb composite monocoque, engine a fully stressed member
design.suspension: Aluminium uprights with carbon-composite double wishbones; pushrod front, pullrod rear
design.concept: Point the exhausts into the diffuser so the car makes downforce from engine gas as well as airflow
design.innovations: The exhaust-blown diffuser, taken further than anyone else and eventually to off-throttle blowing, which kept the effect alive when the driver lifted
design.story: Fifteen poles from nineteen races - the car was on another level over one lap and merely very good over a race distance. Vettel took the championship at the last round in Abu Dhabi having led the standings for exactly none of the season until it ended. Exhaust blowing was progressively restricted and then banned for 2014.
design.outcome: 19 races, 9 wins, 15 poles. Vettel's first title and Red Bull's first constructors' championship.

design.story: The fan was declared to be for cooling, which was true for about 30 per cent of what it did. Lauda won the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix by half a minute and the car was never raced again: Ecclestone owned Brabham and was building his position in FOCA, and the other team principals made withdrawing it the price. It remains the only car to win every Grand Prix it entered.
design.outcome: The BT46B won the one race it started. The conventional BT46 won at Monza the same year.

design.suspension: Front: double wishbone, coil spring and damper. Rear: transverse leaf spring with double wishbone
design.concept: Put the engine behind the driver and the whole car gets smaller, lighter and faster with less power
design.innovations: Not the first rear-engined Grand Prix car, but the one that settled the argument
design.story: Cooper's rear-engined cars had been winning with half the power of a front-engined Ferrari since 1958, and the establishment kept explaining why it did not matter. Brabham's 1959 title ended the discussion: within three seasons every car on the grid had the engine behind the driver, and no front-engined car has won a World Championship race since 1960.
design.outcome: 5 wins. Brabham's 1959 drivers' title and Cooper's 1959 constructors' title - the first for a rear-engined car.

design.story: The F2004 still holds outright lap records at circuits that have not been reprofiled since, which is a strange thing to be able to say about a car from 2004 - modern cars are heavier, on worse tyres, with less engine. design.designers: Colin Chapman, Maurice Philippe
design.power_note: 420-440 bhp at 9,000-10,000 rpm through its life
design.suspension: Front: double wishbone with inboard spring/damper. Rear: top link, lower wishbone and radius rods
design.concept: Bolt the engine straight to the back of the tub and let it be the back of the car
design.innovations: The engine as a fully stressed structural member, carrying the rear suspension; and, from 1968, aerofoil wings mounted on struts to the uprights
design.story: Ford paid Cosworth £100,000 to build the DFV and gave Lotus a year of exclusivity. Clark won first time out at Zandvoort. When the exclusivity lapsed the DFV was sold to anyone who asked, and it went on to win 155 Grands Prix - the reason a small British team with no engine of its own could beat Ferrari for the next fifteen years. The 49 also carried the first wings, which appeared at Monaco in 1968 and were mounted so high and so flimsily that two of them collapsed at Montjuic in 1969.
design.outcome: 12 wins, 19 poles. Hill's 1968 title and Rindt's posthumous 1970 title.

design.story: The fan was declared to be for cooling, which was true for about 30 per cent of what it did. Lauda won the 1978 Swedish Grand Prix by half a minute and the car was never raced again: Ecclestone owned Brabham and was building his position in FOCA, and the other team principals made withdrawing it the price. design.outcome: The BT46B won the one race it started. The conventional BT46 won at Monza the same year.

design.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard coilover. Rear: lower wishbone, top link and radius rod, outboard coilover
design.concept: Replace the tube frame with a stressed aluminium skin: half the weight, three times the stiffness
design.innovations: The first fully stressed monocoque chassis in Formula One, and an extremely low, narrow body around a reclined driving position
design.story: Chapman is said to have sketched it on a napkin. The spaceframe it replaced was a lattice of tubes that had to be triangulated around the driver; the monocoque made the driver's compartment itself the structure. Frontal area came down to 8 square feet. Every serious Formula One car since has been a monocoque of one material or another, and the 25 is the reason.
design.outcome: 14 wins and 14 poles. Clark's 1963 and 1965 titles, with Lotus taking the constructors' championship both years.

design.story: Williams took the 79's idea and out-built its inventor. The FW07 turned a team that had never won a race into a two-time constructors' champion in three seasons and set the pattern for Williams for the next twenty years: someone else's concept, executed better.
design.outcome: 43 races, 15 wins, 8 poles. Jones's 1980 drivers' title; constructors' championships in 1980 and 1981.

design.designers: André de Cortanze, Jean-Pierre Jabouille, François Castaing
design.power_note: About 510 bhp at 11,000 rpm; a single turbo at first, twin turbos later to attack the lag
design.concept: The rules allow 1.5 litres with a turbocharger against 3.0 without; nobody has tried it, so try it
design.innovations: The first turbocharged engine in Formula One, and the first radial tyres
design.story: It was slow, it was unreliable, and rival teams called it the yellow teapot for the cloud of white smoke it produced when it let go, which was often. It never won. But by 1983 every serious car had a turbo, by 1986 there was nothing else on the grid, and the naturally aspirated 3.0-litre engine that had defined Formula One since 1966 was gone.
design.outcome: 25 races, no wins, one pole. The RS10 that followed it won at Dijon in 1979 - the first turbo victory.

design.designers: John Barnard, Alan Jenkins, Steve Nichols
design.power_note: 510 bhp at 11,000 rpm; a TAG-Porsche turbo V6 of about 700 bhp was fitted late in 1983
design.concept: Aluminium is not stiff enough to carry ground-effect loads; build the tub out of carbon fibre instead
design.innovations: The first carbon-fibre composite monocoque to race in Formula One
design.story: Barnard got the idea from Rolls-Royce engineers using carbon fibre in turbofan blades, and had the tub built by Hercules Aerospace in Utah because nobody in motor racing could make one. The paddock thought it would shatter. Then John Watson crashed heavily at Monza in 1981, the car broke apart around a tub that stayed intact, and he walked away. Every car on the grid was carbon-fibre within a few years, and it is the single largest reason drivers stopped dying.
design.outcome: 43 races, 6 wins. No championships - its importance is structural, not competitive.

design.designers: Mauro Forghieri
design.chassis_type: steel tube frame with aluminium shear panels
design.suspension: Front and rear double wishbone, front inboard spring/damper
design.concept: Turn the gearbox sideways and put it ahead of the rear axle line: the mass moves forward and the car turns better
design.innovations: The transverse gearbox - the T in the name is trasversale - which concentrated mass within the wheelbase
design.story: The 312T line ran for six seasons and five designations and is the most successful thing Ferrari built before the Schumacher era. The 312T2 is the car Lauda crashed at the Nürburgring in 1976 and the car he was back in six weeks later. By the 312T5 in 1980 the flat-12 was too wide for ground effect and the car was hopeless - Ferrari finished tenth in the championship, and went turbo.
design.outcome: 89 races, 27 wins, 19 poles. Drivers' titles for Lauda (1975, 1977) and Scheckter (1979); constructors' in 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1979.

design.concept: Bolt the engine straight to the back of the tub and let it be the back of the car

design.story: Ford paid Cosworth £100,000 to build the DFV and gave Lotus a year of exclusivity. Clark won first time out at Zandvoort. When the exclusivity lapsed the DFV was sold to anyone who asked, and it went on to win 155 Grands Prix - the reason a small British team with no engine of its own could beat Ferrari for the next fifteen years. The 49 also carried the first wings, which appeared at Monaco in 1968 and were mounted so high and so flimsily that two of them collapsed at Montjuic in 1969.
design.outcome: 12 wins, 19 poles. Hill's 1968 title and Rindt's posthumous 1970 title.

design.power_note: 220 bhp at 7,400 rpm in 1954, about 240 bhp with fuel injection from 1955; a 315 bhp V12 was offered in 1957 and rarely used
design.suspension: Front: independent wishbone. Rear: de Dion tube
design.concept: The customer car of the 2.5-litre era: not the fastest, but the one anyone could buy and almost anyone could drive
design.story: The 250F is the reason the mid-1950s grids existed at all - Maserati sold them to privateers and they filled out every race for six seasons. Fangio's 1957 German Grand Prix in one is the drive the sport keeps coming back to: a botched pit stop dropped him 48 seconds behind, and he took it all back in 22 laps, breaking the lap record ten times and passing Hawthorn on the last lap.
design.outcome: 8 championship wins across 1954-1960. Fangio's 1954 and 1957 titles.

design.designers: Colin Chapman, Tony Rudd, Tony Southgate, Peter Wright, Martin Ogilvie, Geoff Aldridge
design.power_note: 475 bhp at 11,000 rpm
design.chassis_type: aluminium monocoque, strengthened for ground-effect loads
design.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: parallel top links, lower wishbones, twin radius arms, outboard spring/damper
design.concept: The 78 idea done properly: everything moved out of the airflow under the car so the tunnels run clean from front to back
design.innovations: Full ground effect, with the fuel moved to a single central cell and the rear suspension repackaged to clear the diffuser exits
design.story: The 78 proved the principle; the 79 removed everything that got in its way. Andretti said it was like being painted to the road. It was so far ahead that Chapman had already moved on to the 80, which failed, and then to the twin-chassis 88, which was banned - Lotus never won another championship. Every team copied the 79 for 1979, and Williams and Ligier did it better.
design.outcome: 26 races, 6 wins, 10 poles. Andretti's 1978 title and Lotus's seventh and last constructors' championship.

design.designers: Mauro Forghieri
design.chassis_type: steel tube frame with aluminium shear panels
design.suspension: Front and rear double wishbone, front inboard spring/damper
design.concept: Turn the gearbox sideways and put it ahead of the rear axle line: the mass moves forward and the car turns better
design.innovations: The transverse gearbox - the T in the name is trasversale - which concentrated mass within the wheelbase
design.story: The 312T line ran for six seasons and five designations and is the most successful thing Ferrari built before the Schumacher era. The 312T2 is the car Lauda crashed at the Nürburgring in 1976 and the car he was back in six weeks later. By the 312T5 in 1980 the flat-12 was too wide for ground effect and the car was hopeless - Ferrari finished tenth in the championship, and went turbo.
design.outcome: 89 races, 27 wins, 19 poles. Drivers' titles for Lauda (1975, 1977) and Scheckter (1979); constructors' in 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1979.

design.concept: Give the computer control of the ride height and the car holds its best aerodynamic attitude everywhere, all the time
design.innovations: Active suspension, traction control, semi-automatic gearbox and anti-lock brakes on one car
design.story: The FW14B is the most technologically advanced car ever to race in Formula One, and it is the reason so much of it is now banned. Mansell won the first five races of 1992 and took the title with five rounds left. Active suspension, traction control and launch control were all outlawed for 1994, which is how a technical arms race ends.
design.outcome: 17 wins and 21 poles across the two years. Mansell's 1992 title with nine wins in a season, and the 1992 constructors' championship.

design.designers: John Barnard, Alan Jenkins, Steve Nichols
design.power_note: 510 bhp at 11,000 rpm; a TAG-Porsche turbo V6 of about 700 bhp was fitted late in 1983
design.concept: Aluminium is not stiff enough to carry ground-effect loads; build the tub out of carbon fibre instead
design.innovations: The first carbon-fibre composite monocoque to race in Formula One
design.story: Barnard got the idea from Rolls-Royce engineers using carbon fibre in turbofan blades, and had the tub built by Hercules Aerospace in Utah because nobody in motor racing could make one. The paddock thought it would shatter. Then John Watson crashed heavily at Monza in 1981, the car broke apart around a tub that stayed intact, and he walked away. Every car on the grid was carbon-fibre within a few years, and it is the single largest reason drivers stopped dying.
design.outcome: 43 races, 6 wins. No championships - its importance is structural, not competitive.

design.designers: Ross Brawn, Jörg Zander, Loïc Bigois, John Owen, Masayuki Minagawa (double diffuser)
design.power_note: 750 bhp at 18,000 rpm, the regulation rev limit
design.chassis_type: moulded carbon-fibre and honeycomb composite monocoque
design.suspension: Wishbone and pushrod-activated torsion springs and rockers, front and rear
design.concept: Read the 2009 aerodynamic rewrite more carefully than anyone else and find a second deck in the diffuser that the wording does not forbid
design.innovations: The double diffuser, developed at Honda and inherited when Honda withdrew
design.story: Honda spent a fortune on the 2009 car and then pulled out of Formula One in December 2008. Brawn bought the team for a pound, fitted a Mercedes engine to a chassis designed around a Honda one, and won six of the first seven races. Rivals protested the diffuser and lost at the FIA International Court of Appeal in April. It is the only team to have won the championship in the only season it ever existed - Mercedes bought it at the end of the year.
design.outcome: 17 races, 8 wins, 5 poles. Button's title and the constructors' championship, from a team that did not exist in January and did not exist in the following year.

design.designers: Gioacchino Colombo
design.power_note: Over 300 bhp as the 158 in 1950; about 420 bhp at 9,600 rpm as the 159 in 1951
design.suspension: Front: trailing arm, transverse leaf springs. Rear: swing axle with transverse leaf spring, replaced by a de Dion axle on the 159
design.concept: A pre-war voiturette design, hidden through the war and brought back to win the first two World Championships
design.innovations: Nothing new: the point of the 158 is that a 1938 design was still the best car in the world in 1951
design.story: Alfa entered 1950 with a car designed twelve years earlier and won every race it started. By 1951 it was drinking fuel at about 1.5 miles per gallon and needed two stops where the Ferrari 375 needed one; Fangio won the title anyway, at Barcelona, when Ferrari picked the wrong tyre size. Alfa then withdrew from Grand Prix racing entirely rather than build a successor, which is why 1952 and 1953 were run to Formula Two rules.
design.outcome: Every race entered in 1950; 4 of 7 in 1951. Drivers' titles for Farina and Fangio.

design.designers: Mauro Forghieri
design.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: double wishbone
design.concept: A flat-12 sits low, so the centre of gravity sits low, and the engine can still be a stressed member
design.innovations: The 180-degree flat-12 that Ferrari would use until turbos arrived in 1980
design.story: Forghieri's flat-12 was the answer to the DFV: more power, and mounted so low that it lowered the whole car around it. Its drawback was width, which fought the ground-effect sidepods that arrived at the end of the decade - the reason Ferrari struggled in 1979-80 while Williams and Lotus flew.
design.outcome: 10 wins across the 312B, B2 and B3. The B3-74 took Lauda to the 1975 title and Ferrari to the constructors'.

design.designers: Mauro Forghieri
design.chassis_type: steel tube frame with aluminium shear panels
design.suspension: Front and rear double wishbone, front inboard spring/damper
design.concept: Turn the gearbox sideways and put it ahead of the rear axle line: the mass moves forward and the car turns better
design.innovations: The transverse gearbox - the T in the name is trasversale - which concentrated mass within the wheelbase
design.story: The 312T line ran for six seasons and five designations and is the most successful thing Ferrari built before the Schumacher era. The 312T2 is the car Lauda crashed at the Nürburgring in 1976 and the car he was back in six weeks later. By the 312T5 in 1980 the flat-12 was too wide for ground effect and the car was hopeless - Ferrari finished tenth in the championship, and went turbo.
design.outcome: 89 races, 27 wins, 19 poles. Drivers' titles for Lauda (1975, 1977) and Scheckter (1979); constructors' in 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1979.

design.designers: Rudolf Uhlenhaut
design.power_note: 257 bhp on debut, developed towards 290-300 bhp; a 340 bhp target at 10,000 rpm was never reached in a race
design.suspension: Front: double wishbone with torsion bars. Rear: low-pivot swing axle with torsion bars
design.concept: Aircraft engineering applied to a racing car: direct fuel injection, desmodromic valves, and a full-width streamliner body
design.innovations: Direct fuel injection taken from Daimler-Benz aero engines; desmodromic valve gear, which closes the valves mechanically instead of with springs and so removes the rev ceiling that valve float imposes; inboard brakes; the Type Monza streamliner
design.story: The only closed-wheel car ever to win a World Championship race, and it won three. Mercedes ran the streamliner at fast circuits and an open-wheel body elsewhere after Fangio complained he could not place the front wheels at Silverstone. The programme ended abruptly after Le Mans 1955, where a Mercedes sports car went into the crowd and killed more than eighty people; Mercedes did not return to Formula One as a constructor until 2010.
design.outcome: 9 wins from 12 races entered. Fangio's titles in 1954 and 1955.

design.designers: Mauro Forghieri
design.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: double wishbone
design.concept: A flat-12 sits low, so the centre of gravity sits low, and the engine can still be a stressed member
design.innovations: The 180-degree flat-12 that Ferrari would use until turbos arrived in 1980
design.story: Forghieri's flat-12 was the answer to the DFV: more power, and mounted so low that it lowered the whole car around it. Its drawback was width, which fought the ground-effect sidepods that arrived at the end of the decade - the reason Ferrari struggled in 1979-80 while Williams and Lotus flew.
design.outcome: 10 wins across the 312B, B2 and B3. The B3-74 took Lauda to the 1975 title and Ferrari to the constructors'.

design.designers: Colin Chapman, Peter Wright, Tony Rudd, Martin Ogilvie
design.suspension: Top rocker arms, lower wishbones, inboard springs front and rear
design.concept: Two chassis, one inside the other: the outer one takes the aerodynamic load and runs stiff, the inner one carries the driver and rides softly
design.innovations: The twin-chassis principle, and one of the first extensive uses of carbon fibre in a chassis
design.story: Ground-effect cars had to run rock-hard suspension to keep the skirts sealed, which by 1981 was punishing enough to hurt drivers. Chapman's answer separated the two jobs. Rival teams protested that the sprung outer body was a movable aerodynamic device; the car was excluded from three race weekends and never started a Grand Prix. It is the clearest case in the sport's history of a rule stopping a genuinely good idea, and Chapman's disgust at it is usually read as the beginning of the end of Lotus.
design.outcome: Never raced. Ran in practice at Long Beach, Rio and Silverstone in 1981 and was excluded each time.

design.designers: Bob Bell, Aldo Costa, Geoff Willis, John Owen, Mike Elliott, Loïc Serra
design.power_note: About 840 bhp combined at up to 15,000 rpm, from a 1.6-litre V6 plus MGU-K and MGU-H
design.chassis_type: moulded carbon-fibre and honeycomb composite monocoque
design.suspension: Carbon-fibre wishbones, pushrod front and pullrod rear, actuating torsion springs
design.concept: Split the turbocharger in half and put the compressor at the front of the V and the turbine at the back, joined by a shaft through the vee
design.innovations: The split-turbo layout, which shortened the intake path, cooled the charge air better and packaged the whole power unit tighter than anything else on the grid
design.story: The 2014 hybrid rules were the biggest engine change since 1989 and Mercedes had understood them years earlier. The split turbo is the single decision that bought them the next eight constructors' championships: Ferrari and Renault had to redesign around it and were years catching up. Hamilton and Rosberg won 16 of 19 races and finished first and second in the championship.
design.outcome: 19 races, 16 wins, 18 poles. Hamilton's second title and the first of eight consecutive Mercedes constructors' championships.

design.concept: The most complete exploitation of the 2022 ground-effect rules: low drag on the straights without giving anything up in the corners
design.story: Twenty-one wins from twenty-two races, beating the MP4/4's 93.8 per cent with 95.5 per cent, and leading 86.7 per cent of all laps run. The one it lost was Singapore. Verstappen won ten in a row, a record. It is the most dominant single season any car has had, and it happened under a cost cap that was supposed to prevent exactly this.
design.outcome: 22 races, 21 wins. Verstappen's third title and Red Bull's sixth constructors' championship.

design.designers: John Barnard, Alan Jenkins, Steve Nichols
design.power_note: 510 bhp at 11,000 rpm; a TAG-Porsche turbo V6 of about 700 bhp was fitted late in 1983
design.concept: Aluminium is not stiff enough to carry ground-effect loads; build the tub out of carbon fibre instead
design.innovations: The first carbon-fibre composite monocoque to race in Formula One
design.story: Barnard got the idea from Rolls-Royce engineers using carbon fibre in turbofan blades, and had the tub built by Hercules Aerospace in Utah because nobody in motor racing could make one. The paddock thought it would shatter. Then John Watson crashed heavily at Monza in 1981, the car broke apart around a tub that stayed intact, and he walked away. Every car on the grid was carbon-fibre within a few years, and it is the single largest reason drivers stopped dying.
design.outcome: 43 races, 6 wins. No championships - its importance is structural, not competitive.

design.story: Williams took the 79's idea and out-built its inventor. The FW07 turned a team that had never won a race into a two-time constructors' champion in three seasons and set the pattern for Williams for the next twenty years: someone else's concept, executed better.
design.outcome: 43 races, 15 wins, 8 poles. Jones's 1980 drivers' title; constructors' championships in 1980 and 1981.

lotus-88.susp_front: Top rocker arms, lower wishbones, inboard springs

design.designers: Colin Chapman, Peter Wright, Tony Rudd, Martin Ogilvie
design.suspension: Top rocker arms, lower wishbones, inboard springs front and rear
design.concept: Two chassis, one inside the other: the outer one takes the aerodynamic load and runs stiff, the inner one carries the driver and rides softly
design.innovations: The twin-chassis principle, and one of the first extensive uses of carbon fibre in a chassis
design.story: Ground-effect cars had to run rock-hard suspension to keep the skirts sealed, which by 1981 was punishing enough to hurt drivers. Chapman's answer separated the two jobs. Rival teams protested that the sprung outer body was a movable aerodynamic device; the car was excluded from three race weekends and never started a Grand Prix. It is the clearest case in the sport's history of a rule stopping a genuinely good idea, and Chapman's disgust at it is usually read as the beginning of the end of Lotus.
design.outcome: Never raced. Ran in practice at Long Beach, Rio and Silverstone in 1981 and was excluded each time.

ferrari-312t5.name: 312T5
ferrari-312t5.chassis_type: Steel tube frame with aluminium shear panels

design.designers: Mauro Forghieri
design.chassis_type: steel tube frame with aluminium shear panels
design.suspension: Front and rear double wishbone, front inboard spring/damper
design.concept: Turn the gearbox sideways and put it ahead of the rear axle line: the mass moves forward and the car turns better
design.innovations: The transverse gearbox - the T in the name is trasversale - which concentrated mass within the wheelbase
design.story: The 312T line ran for six seasons and five designations and is the most successful thing Ferrari built before the Schumacher era. The 312T2 is the car Lauda crashed at the Nürburgring in 1976 and the car he was back in six weeks later. By the 312T5 in 1980 the flat-12 was too wide for ground effect and the car was hopeless - Ferrari finished tenth in the championship, and went turbo.
design.outcome: 89 races, 27 wins, 19 poles. Drivers' titles for Lauda (1975, 1977) and Scheckter (1979); constructors' in 1975, 1976, 1977 and 1979.

design.designers: Colin Chapman, Tony Rudd, Ralph Bellamy, Peter Wright, Martin Ogilvie
design.suspension: Front: double wishbone, inboard spring/damper. Rear: parallel top links, lower wishbones, twin radius arms
design.concept: Shape the underside of the sidepods as inverted wings and seal the edges: the car makes downforce without making drag
design.innovations: Ground effect, and sliding skirts to seal the low-pressure area at the car's edges
design.story: Wings make downforce and pay for it in drag. Peter Wright's insight was that the whole underbody could be a wing instead, and that the ground itself would double the effect if the sides were sealed. The 78 was quick everywhere and unbeatable in slow corners. It should have won the 1977 championship and did not, because the DFV kept failing.
design.outcome: 7 wins and 9 poles across 1977 and early 1978, before the 79 replaced it.
